description: >-
  Orchestrated red/green build with a scored cross-model review loop (Opus
  orchestrates, Sonnet and Sol implement, Sol or Opus review, Fable decides
  round 3) and triage of upstream review-bot comments. One working Claude
  agent at a time; reviewers have their own cap of one; only the owner raises

---

# build-loop

**After compaction: reread this skill.** A summary keeps the task but loses
these rules. When a session that used build-loop comes back from compaction,
reread this file, `vigil` and the reference for the step you are on before any other step. If work is in
flight, re-arm a vigil hold and start its background keepalive in that turn (§10). Compaction summaries preserve the reread and live-hold requirement.

This file is a router; detail lives in `references/`. Section numbers are stable.

**Load the companions.**

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | Before design or code, and when judging a finding. |
| `test-quality` | Before red, when tests come back, when a fix touches a test. |
| `question-everything` | Before a spec and before green (§4a). |
| `vigil` | As soon as work is in flight (§10); `manual-keepalive` only if vigil fails. |
| `qex`, `low-ram-hosts` | Before any heavy job (§8–9). |

**Load the references at their step.**

| File | Read it |
|---|---|
| `references/phases.md` | Before §3, before launching red, before green. |
| `references/roles.md`, `references/dialogue.md` | Before every implementer or reviewer brief; roles also on budget advice or reset. |
| `references/review.md`, `-v2.md` | Before review round 1 (§6: bar, rounds, checkpoint, answering, ledger, v2 schedule). |
| `references/bars.md` | At `review-ledger init`, to choose the bar (§6a). |
| `references/bots.md` | When a PR bot posts (§6e). |
| `references/sol.md` | Before the first Sol run (§7). |
| `references/scoping.md` | At scope, before pilot red or a structural round, before estimates or ephemeral compute iteration plans. |
| `references/budget.md` | On budget advice, a usage limit or reset, before a second agent, on a vigil `item overdue` (§8–§10). |
| `references/reviewers.md` | Before a contribution to a project you do not own, before re-scoping a PR after review. |
| `references/handoff.md` | Before a PR body or the final report (§11–§12). |

Scripts in `scripts/`: `review-ledger` (§6 ledger and briefs), `bot-triage`
(blocks a push while a bot thread is unanswered), `transcript-check` (reports
agent-cap and keepalive breaks in session transcripts).

## Dialogue before work advances

Every agent reviewer, including spec and final reviewers and clean approvals,
needs at least one substantive argument exchange with the orchestrator per round.
Fable needs at least two; keep the existing two-exchange rule on non-clean round 4.
Challenge an assumption or explain why a simpler design suffices; do not invent
disagreement. Implementers start work immediately. Roughly five minutes in,
the orchestrator reads 1–5 relevant files, asks about ambiguities and 2–3
work-grounded questions, hears the answers, then pushes back and settles the
direction. Short batches get this check at handoff. Details: `dialogue.md`.

Every brief states most-important behavior, invariants, priority concerns, lower
priorities and evidence. Preserve serious defects regardless of priority. Use
`references/dialogue.md` and the ledger to record focus and dialogue. No upfront
proposal approval.

## 0. Boldness

Put this in your stance and every implementer prompt:

> Remember that you are motherfucking powerful. You need to go full gas, balls to the wall. Get this crazy shit done. Be ambitious. Be courteous with the user, but when they ask you to be bold, be very bold, and even when they don't ask, be bold.

Bold means big, well-aimed batches and firm pushback on weak findings, never
skipping verification, scope control or approval gates. Boldness never raises
the agent cap (§2): bold means a bigger, better-aimed single run.

**Stance (owner 2026-11-13).** If you think this is a good idea, do it.
Otherwise, suggest something else. Tell the owner when they are about to do
something dumb. On judgement calls (scope, design, worth fixing) weigh Fable's
unusual claims more than Sol's; a test settles facts, not either model.

## 1. Feature discussion (before any engineering)

Do this first, in order:

0. **Scope.** Ask: a pilot (a few cases, gather data, then decide), a
   structural fix, or hardening? Default: pilot; ask inline and
   keep working (§1a). A pilot gets its own branch and stays a reference; the
   structural round starts fresh. Pilot rules: `references/scoping.md`. Until hardening,
   test the design, not the symptom; every implementer brief carries the 30-minute flag and "never vigil orchestrator mode".
1. **Simpler alternative.** Does a simpler way exist (do less, reuse, change
   the requirement)?
2. **Desires.** Their first-order desire (what they asked for), second-order
   desire (why), and threat model (who can reach it, untrusted inputs, what it holds).
3. **Debate Socratically.** Question assumptions and offer counter-cases and
   cheaper options. Then write the agreed intent in 1-2 sentences: the review
   brief's Intent.

Skip only for a fix whose intent is already unambiguous. If the user may be
away, take the sensible default and log it (§1a). Poorly scoped work: ask for
more detail first (`question-everything`).

## 1a. Owner contact and decisions

Assume the user is away: ask inline with a default and keep working.
AskUserQuestion only on request: it blocks. Never block; take the safe default and log it as "Defaults taken" (`references/roles.md`).

## 2. Roles and budget

**Agent cap.** One working Claude agent (Opus, Sonnet, Fable, Haiku) at a time.
Reviewers have a separate cap of one. Only the owner raises the cap; log the
raise with an end condition (a time or a task), and when it ends, count again
before every launch. Implementers, authors, researchers, integrators, spec
writers and investigators all count, and changing model or role never changes
the cap. "Economical" means usage first, wall-clock second, so parallel authors
are never economical. If one owner message holds several requests, state an
order and run them one after another. This cap outranks the harness's general
advice to parallelise. Before every `delegate_task` or Agent call, check in one
line: working Claude agents now (`vigil status <hold>` lists the items; count the Claude-run ones; Codex/Sol
runs and commands do not count, reviewers count against their own cap) are under the cap, and the
run serves the owner's priority workstream, else queue it. Codex and Sol runs
are less strict: run them in parallel when it helps, but watch their limits,
which run out faster now.

| Role | Default | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | Opus (you) | Specs, prompts, verification, commits, pushes, owner contact. Writes little code. |
| Implementer | Sonnet and Sol, alternating by fix round (B1) | Red tests, green code, fixes. |
| Reviewer, rounds 1-2 | Sol or Opus | Scored fix rounds (§6). Reviews only, plus comment fixups. |
| Reviewer, round 3 | Fable 5.2 or later | The "good enough to ship" call (§6). |
| Reviewer, tier 2 | Fresh Opus (Fable if Opus wrote code) | One pass on the stable diff. |

B1–B5, R2 (a reviewer never reviews code it wrote), C3, budget switching and
batching: `references/roles.md`. Never quietly substitute a model for a role
the user pinned. State who holds which role at the start of each phase.

## 3–5. Scope, red, spec gate, green

Find the base, ONE diff command (§3). One red run for the whole scope; verify
the red gate yourself, commit red (§4). Spec gate before green (§4a). Green in
batches, verified and committed per phase (§5). Shared tree: `git commit
--only -- <paths>`; never stash. Steps: `references/phases.md`.

## 6. Review loop (scored, bounded)

After green, or before filing a PR, review runs across model families, then
bots get triaged (§6e). **Read `references/review.md` and
`references/review-v2.md` before round 1**; drive the rounds with
`scripts/review-ledger`.

Stages: pilot → structural → hardening. Pilots use agreed bars, round-2 Fable and owner approval; see `scoping.md`. Integration branches the owner runs need structural review; upstream PRs and project releases need hardening.

Rounds 1–2 use Sol or Opus, excluding authors. Round 3 uses Fable, then a
step-back if needed. Rounds 4–5 follow the documented pivot schedule; stop
stuck after five. Each round completes its argument minimum before advancing.
The pilot schedule, score bars, checkpoint, cull and final-fix rules remain in
`references/review-v2.md`.

Tier 2 is a fresh Opus pass, or Fable if Opus wrote code. After a passing
Fable round there is no tier 2. A ledger without `schema: 2` keeps the legacy
schedule. Run Sol per §7; run Opus as a subagent (`model: opus`) with the
review-only brief and no history. In `references/`: **6a** replies carry
`SCORE[concern]: n/10` against bars; only `needed for bar: yes` blocks; **6b** full diff in round 1, then diff-only
(a timeout is not approval); **6c** which layer stops each bug class; **6d**
smallest fix, failing test first, never agree to end the loop; **6e** PR bots,
`bot-triage guard` before each push; **A7** comment fixups only.

## 7. Running Sol

T3 `delegate_task` first, then `codex`; no Sol route: report the blocker,
substitute no model. `references/sol.md`.

## 8–9. Usage limits and concurrency

On a usage limit: save partial work, wait for the reset, probe, resume; never
restart. The cap is §2. Heavy work runs on ephemeral compute, the few local
jobs through qex. Extra implementers get their own worktree; forbid `git
stash`. `references/budget.md`, `references/scoping.md`.

## 10. Keepalive and low-budget conduct

**Hold the session with vigil** while anything is in flight, even with nothing
to watch: each wait also checks usage limits and advisories. Manual tick only
if vigil is unavailable or failing; never loops or chained sleeps.

**Wait in the background:** `vigil keepalive <hold> --orchestrator`,
`run_in_background`, timeout at least 3,600,000 ms; on each return, act and
start the next. Subagents never use orchestrator mode. One session hold
(bare is fine); each delegated run is an item: `vigil hold add <hold> --for
pid:N|file:<report>|none --expect-s N --label <run>`, and `vigil hold done
<hold> <run>` on a `none` run's notification. Never cancel it; if it
releases, make a new hold in the same turn.

"In flight": a working or paused subagent, Sol run or reviewer; a background
command; a wait on CI, a bot or a usage reset; queued work; or the user asked
(only they end it). Never end a turn with work in flight and no live hold.

Long jobs and low budget: `references/budget.md` §10.

## 11. Ship

Push only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR; never during the
loop. Outward actions (PRs, comments, upstream pushes) need approval; show the
draft first. PR body line: `references/handoff.md`.

## 12. Hand-off report

Contents: `references/handoff.md`.

# Notification flow pilot

## Intent and scope

Make the owner's notification categories, schedules, and budgets responsive and reliable on the existing `rework` pilot. Preserve explicit cancellation, spend only on actual delivery, default to recent notifications, add automation, and replace the window editor with a focused timeline. Snoozing and original-source icons are opt-in experiments, each independently disableable. No upstream publication or broad reskin is included.

Base: `8b7c2ece17344402737dd7b567f7e139df8f826a`. This branch is itself a pilot, as explicitly requested by the owner on 2026-11-17. Retain it as a reference if a later structural implementation starts fresh. Earlier audit and diagnostic tooling are part of the preparation checkpoint.

## Owner decisions

- Only explicit notification cancellation clears queued notifications. Opening an app alone does not.
- Cleared before delivery costs zero. Clearing a delivered notification does not refund spending.
- Notification priority precedes per-app queue preference. App queue preference cannot override it.
- Newest first is the default; apps may opt into oldest first and a higher position within the same notification priority.
- Retain distinct older notifications. Updates to a pending notification replace its contents and move it according to its updated recency.
- Optimize both category/app management and the inbox/dashboard, including scrolling.
- Schedule intents choose repeating or dated mode. Omitted mode defaults to repeating.
- Budget/window edits preserve spending already incurred. Spent 6, new budget 10 means 4 remaining.
- Manual and automated edits use last change wins.
- Windows continuously cover the entire local day, with shared boundaries and a one-hour minimum.
- A newly split window goes immediately after the focused window. Two adjacent 90-minute windows can become three adjacent one-hour windows, including borrowing from the preceding neighbor when the focused window is the latter.
- Failure to find enough time shows an error dialog with instructions for enlarging suitable windows.
- Preserve Edge's fast drag, hold for minute precision, and zoom controls.

## Delivery and cancellation contract

One coordinator must serialize arrival, explicit clearing, and scheduled delivery decisions. Recheck pending state at authorization; a stale batch snapshot must not resurrect a cleared row. Preserve cancellation information when asynchronous arrival processing would otherwise overwrite a newer removal. Farhan's own interception/snoozing removal is not an explicit source-app cancellation. Distinguish removal reasons.

Budget spending and delivered state must remain consistent across overlapping immediate/batch attempts and repeated callbacks. A notification key already delivered must not spend again solely because its contents update. Define the durable decision and notification-post failure boundary explicitly; notification manager effects cannot participate in a Room transaction. Do not advertise exactly-once delivery across a crash without evidence. On a posting failure, do not report a successful delivery or permanently lose its budget allowance.

Queue order: notification priority, per-app queue rank, then candidate recency. Within a priority/rank group, choose the head of each app's queue according to that app's newest/oldest policy; compare eligible heads by recency with deterministic ties. A configurable FIFO app must not bypass higher-priority items. Stable notification keys identify updates; timestamps alone do not identify distinct notifications.

Bound action-store ownership and make mutations safe across service/UI coroutines. Release eligible tap/reply/proxy entries on deletion and clearing, including clear-all. Preserve queued actions needed for delivery. Avoid new background polling for cleanup or source discovery.

## Schedule model and automation

Represent the day as [0, 1440) minutes, displaying the final boundary as 24:00. The current 23:59 endpoint omits a minute and must migrate without losing saved budgets. Reject malformed fields, overlaps, gaps, negative budgets, and windows shorter than 60 minutes. Every entry point uses the same validator and write path. Valid changes are atomic; invalid automation leaves the saved schedule and spend unchanged.

Repeating schedules use the phone's local wall clock. Dated overrides target one explicit ISO local date and use the repeating schedule on other dates. Last successfully accepted write wins for its applicable scope. A repeating write supersedes the currently applicable dated override so a manual edit is not silently hidden. Repeating/dated intent replay must not refill spending. Date and timezone tests use explicit clocks/zones; no 86,400-second assumption for calendar days.

Keep an accounting identity independent of editable boundary positions. Moving, splitting, merging, or reapplying a currently active window must not manufacture a new budget allowance. Natural passage into a new window/day may reset its allowance. Specify how an accepted edit changes that transition, preserving current spending; prove with tests.

Provide a versioned explicit Android intent contract suitable for Tasker: payload is a complete validated schedule plus mode and optional local date. Default mode is repeating. No automatic sensor integration is included. Acknowledgement/error must be observable without exposing notification content. External automation is opt-in and authenticated with a locally generated credential that the owner can copy/revoke; do not place the credential or private notification content in logs. Bound payload size and reject unknown versions. Document action, receiver, fields, date behavior, replacement behavior, examples, and validation errors from the shipped implementation.

## Timeline editor

Reference: Edge `pilot/sleep-editor-fixes` at `e0759a67f`, `lib/ui2/day_timeline/timeline_model.dart` and its shared timeline widgets. Implement in native Compose; do not import Flutter.

Select a zone to edit its budget. Select a shared boundary before dragging it. Only the focused boundary is draggable; selection itself must not change time. Clamp movement to keep both adjacent zones at least 60 minutes. Fast dragging rounds to five-minute increments. Holding still for 600 ms activates one-minute increments at quarter-speed, anchored at the current value without a jump. Include zoom-in, zoom-out/reset, panning as needed, visible exact time, and accessible non-drag time controls. Full-day coverage never changes with zoom.

Splitting defaults, chosen from the owner's examples:

Dated-today, replacing today's override, tomorrow, replay, and moving now across a boundary have controls.

The listener copies bounded relevant fields into one 128-entry mailbox. It captures monotonic callback order before IO; it does not launch a coroutine or retain a StatusBarNotification per arrival. The owner found a real defect in the initial global `uncertain(key)` guard: once a callback token was evicted, arbitrary historical pending rows could remain deferred forever. That guard is removed.

# Boat

Boat (boat.dev) rents full Linux VMs ("sandboxes"): x86_64 Ubuntu, user
`user`, home `/home/user`, passwordless `sudo`, Docker and common toolchains,
billed per second while running. Older docs and third-party skills call it
**Box** (`box` CLI, `box.ascii.dev`, `on.ascii.dev`): same product, stale
names. Use `boat`. Inside a sandbox, agents get Boat's own `boat` skill; this
one is for driving sandboxes from here.

## Access

- The CLI is `boat` (on `PATH`; `~/.ascii/bin/boat`) and is already signed in:
  `boat status`. Never run `boat login`, `boat onboard` or an install script;
  if it says signed out, ask the user.
- A sandbox is reachable **only through the CLI** (`exec`, `ssh`, `scp`,
  `forward`). It is not on Tailscale and has no entry in `~/.ssh/config`.
- Always pass the explicit `bx_...` id. `current` and `self` do not work from
  a non-interactive shell here.
- Which sandbox: read `<project>.research/boat.md` (id, purpose, size, what
  secrets it holds). Update it when you create, trim or retire one.

## Commands

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| State, size, TTL | `boat info <id>` (JSON; fields under `.sandbox`), `boat list` |
| Start / stop | `boat resume <id>`, `boat stop <id>` |
| Short command | `boat exec <id> --timeout 120 -- bash -lc '<cmd>'` (default timeout 30 s) |
| Long job | `boat exec <id> --detach -- bash -lc '<cmd> > ~/job.log 2>&1'` → prints `pid` |
| Wait for it | `boat exec <id> --attach <pid>` as a background Bash command (the harness notifies you); `--status <pid>`, `--kill <pid>` |
| Files | `boat scp ./f <id>:/home/user/f`, `boat scp <id>:/home/user/f ./f` |
| Source | `git bundle create x.bundle <branch>`, `scp` it, `git clone x.bundle` inside: no Git credentials enter the sandbox |
| Plan and hours | `boat limits`, `boat usage <id>`; never quote prices from memory |

`exec` prints one JSON line (`stdout`, `stderr`, exit code). Parse it, for
example `| python3 -c 'import json,sys; d=json.loads(sys.stdin.readline()); print(d["stdout"])'`.

## Gotchas seen here

- **Nix socket after resume.** The first Nix call after `resume` fails with
  "Permission denied" on the daemon socket. A plain restart can leave the
  socket at mode 0644, and a `chmod 666` alone later gives "Connection refused"
  once a detached job starts. What works (one `exec`): `sudo systemctl stop
  nix-daemon.service nix-daemon.socket; sudo rm -f
  /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket; sudo systemctl start nix-daemon.socket
  nix-daemon.service; sleep 3; sudo chmod 666
  /nix/var/nix/daemon-socket/socket; nix store ping`. Then run detached jobs
  under `setpriv` (below). Source
  `/nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh` in each `exec`.
- **Capabilities.** `exec` processes carry ambient capabilities that break
  FHS/bubblewrap tools. Wrap detached runs:
  `--detach -- setpriv --ambient-caps -all --inh-caps -all bash -lc '...'`.
- **Nothing survives a stop** except the disk: relaunch services after
  `resume`. The IP changes on each resume.
- **Size.** Boat counts allocated disk; a sandbox past the default limit needs
  `--type large` to resume (2× cost). Trim or `nix-store --gc` instead of
  upsizing, and ask before choosing a paid size.
- **Memory.** Sandboxes have their own RAM (the qex queue is for this host),
  but default size is ~8 GB: one Gradle or emulator job at a time.

- **Secrets stay put.** Never copy keys, tokens or signing keystores into a

# Running on RAM-constrained hosts (sonic and nixed)

**Both sonic and nixed need this.** Neither is a big machine:

| Host | RAM | Swap |
|------|-----|------|
| sonic (CF-19, x86_64) | 8GB | zram + disk swap partition |
| nixed (M1, aarch64) | ~7.4GB | zram (3.7GB) + 8GB swapfile |

void has plenty of memory; this skill is not for it.

Agents here (t3, Claude Code, Codex sessions) share the same memory as
whatever test or build they launch. One runaway test can use 6GB on its own,
and the machine then swaps hard or the kernel OOM killer fires.

## Why it matters

The kernel kills the biggest process, which is usually the runaway test, not
the agents. On nixed, `flutter_tester` (~6GB) was killed three times on
2026-10-18. Before `OOMPolicy=continue` was set on `t3.service`, systemd then
stopped the whole unit and every agent session in it died too. That setting
is now in `scout-modules/t3`, but the box is still thrashing the whole time
before the kill. Keep tests small and capped so it never comes to that.

## Heavy work goes to Boat first

**Prefer Boat (cloud sandboxes) for all heavy work**: test runs beyond one or
two files, suites, builds, APKs, long benchmarks. Use
`edge.research/bin/boat-run [--shell PREFIX] <worktree> -- <command>`: it syncs
the worktree, fixes the Nix socket, runs detached and returns the exit code and
the log (see the `boat` skill). Queuing heavy runs in qex on these 8GB hosts
cost 20 to 120 minutes of waiting on 2026-11-11, and Boat has no memory
problem. Briefs to subagents name `boat-run`, not a local runner.
Boat spends plan hours: use the boat skill's "Spend" table (cheap by default: `default`
size for test iterations, sandbox stops itself between batches; `large` and keep-up only under an
owner deadline).

Use qex on this host only:

- for one or two quick runs (a single test file, a small build), or
- when the `boat-budget` vigil advisory says Boat is low: Boat's remaining
  hours are at or below the threshold (default 10%). Read it with `vigil advice`
  (it is also in every `keepalive` result's `advice`). The threshold is
  `vigil advisory set boat-budget threshold=<percent>`. If the advice says it
  is unavailable, prefer Boat and check `boat limits` yourself.

## Queue the local jobs through qex

Whatever stays local (see above) goes through the queue. Agents can't see what
other agents are about to start. On 2026-11-10 two
sessions' Rust and Gradle builds plus a test run caused 8 OOM kills in 25
minutes on nixed. `qex` is the shared queue: a job claims cores and memory,
and qex starts it only when the claim fits the budget (75% of the machine,
less what other users hold). Load the `qex` skill, or run `qex help agents`.

```sh
qex list                 # who holds what now, and why anything waits
qex info                 # the budget and the load
qex submit --wait --cpu 2 --mem 3GB --id-file /tmp/<you>.id -- <command>
```

- Run `qex submit --wait` as a background command of your harness; the harness
  reports the end. Reattach with `qex status $(cat <id-file>) --wait`. No
  pgrep or sleep loops.
- Claim what the job really uses. Starting points on these hosts: `flutter
  test` 2GB, Gradle/APK build 3GB, `cargo build -j2` 2GB, `nix build` 2GB.
  qex learns from each run of the same command.
- A claim is a promise, not a limit. Put the scope cap below inside the job:
  `qex submit --wait --mem 3GB -- systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=4G -- <command>`.
- Never skip the queue because it is slow. A waiting job is cheaper than an
  OOM kill of someone else's work.
- But a job that has waited for memory for more than ~20 minutes should move
  to Boat instead (cancel it with `qex cancel <id>`). A queued job is still
  in flight: keep the keepalive tick live while it waits.

Source: edge "live guides r2" (2026-11-13) and "no-spinners" (2026-11-15).

## The scope question (§1)

Ask the owner which kind of change this is:

- **Pilot**: try it on a few cases, gather data, then decide.
- **Structural fix**: change how the thing works everywhere.
- **Hardening**: strengthen the structural design before an upstream PR or project release.

**Default: pilot.** Owner: "The answer is typically launch things as pilots first, because then we're
able to gather more data and that data is able to inform implementations that are correct the first
time." Ask inline with that default and keep working (§1a). A bug fix is not a pilot; skip the
question when the kind is obvious.

## Pilot rules

- **Scored, agreed before starting (owner, 2026-11-15).** Agree the feature's scored concerns and
  bars with the owner, typically four: data safety (`durability`), correctness (`error-paths`), the
  feature goal (`legibility` for UX, `performance` for layout shift), maintainability (`architecture`).
  Record exactly those concerns at init, for example `init --pilot --bar durability=9 --bar wiring=7
  --bars-agreed "<owner quote or note>"`. Concern names come from `bars.md`.
  Without an agreement, touched concerns default to 6, except durability at 7. If the pilot writes
  stored data, changes schema or migrations, or sends notifications or other outward messages,
  pass `--touches-data`: durability
  defaults to 9 and is included automatically. `durable-state`/`migration` categories also select it.
  Init prints the default applied. Pilots never record or constrain a region's shape/stage in
  `bars.json`. Structural and later stages keep the normal shape × stage bars.
- **Review schedule.** Round 1: Sol or Opus, never the author. Round 2: Fable, including ARGUE,
  STEP-BACK, NIT-CULL and FIX-KEPT; later rounds keep the normal caps. Every named concern must
  meet its bar, and the owner must approve the pilot build. Record `review-ledger -l L owner-ok
  "<quote>"`; without it the ledger refuses CHECKPOINT and STOP-AGREED.
- **Hardening list.** Use the existing `HARDENING-STASH`, not a second list. Review briefs send
  findings outside the agreed concerns, or not needed for the current bars, there. Do not fix them
  this round. Typical items: pixel/frame tests and sweeps, stricter measurement, micro-performance,
  screen readers, translations of changing copy, maintainability tidy-ups.
- **Tests cover the pilot's own cases only.** No sweeps over every item, no catalogue-wide guards,
  until the owner decides to go structural. Size check: pilot test code stays under about twice the
  expected change. Over that, cut tests before writing more.
- **No full test runs (owner, 2026-11-15).** The pilot stage runs targeted tests and gates for what
  it touches. Full runs belong to the structural and hardening stages.
- **One red round.** The spec review (§4a) may run alongside green, not before it. Its findings go to
  the first fix round.
- **Ship iteration builds early.** An iteration build, preview or screenshot set goes to the owner as soon as the
  targeted tests pass. The pilot's scored review (§6) follows the owner's feedback.
- **Opt-in.** Put pilot behaviour behind a flag or a per-item field, so the pilot build changes only
  the pilot's cases.
- **Own branch, kept as a reference (owner, 2026-11-15).** Keep the pilot branch as a reference.
  Start the structural stage fresh from the base on a new branch, carrying over only the code,
  tests and evidence the owner endorsed. Pilot tests encode the pilot design; rebuilding avoids
  spending the structural round undoing it.
- **End with evidence** for the owner's decision: before/after shots, counts, what broke.

Structural and hardening stages use the normal bars and review schedule (§4–§6).

## Stages and what to test (§1, §3)

The work stages are pilot → structural → hardening:

- **Pilot**: a few cases, opt-in; tests cover the pilot's own cases only (above).
- **Structural**: the owner says go wide. One design check per fix; looser on edge cases.
- **Hardening**: before an upstream PR opens or goes ready, or a project release, review the
  hardening stash at normal bars. Add symptom tests, catalogue sweeps, pixel/frame tests, edge cases.

Before a structural round lands on an integration branch the owner runs: the structural review
at normal bars, Fable at round 3, no extra triage. Before an upstream PR or a project release: hardening.

**Test the design, not the symptom, until hardening.** When a fix rules a bug out by construction,
one assertion that the construction is in place is the test. Symptom tests (frame stepping, pixel
sampling, timing, sweeps over every item) are hardening work.

**30-minute flag.** An implementer that spends more than 30 minutes on one problem (the same failing
test or symptom across 3 or more runs) flags it to the orchestrator in its report and keeps working on
the rest. The orchestrator cuts it (defers it to hardening) or asks the owner. Put this rule in every
implementer brief, next to: "You may use vigil, but never orchestrator mode (`orchestrator: true` /
`--orchestrator`); that is only for the main session that talks with the user."

## 1. Rich interfaces

An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:

| Part | Says |
|---|---|
| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |

**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus

Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.

Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):

```
// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
...
// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
ack(token);
```

- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.

- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).

# Test quality

A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |

## 1. Every test says why

The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.

```
// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
```

- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
  claim's grep finds its proof.
- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
  candidate.
- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).

## 2. Placement

Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
suites live apart, and say so in their why.

## 3. Techniques worth using

### Monoids and accumulators
If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:

| Law | Property |
|---|---|
| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |

/** Local opt-in credential owner. UI may copy/rotate/revoke it; no credential enters logs or tracing. */
@Singleton
class ScheduleAutomationCredentials @Inject constructor(private val preferences: SharedPreferences) : AutomationCredentials {
    override fun isEnabled(): Boolean = preferences.getBoolean(ENABLED, false)
    override fun matches(presented: String?): Boolean {
        val saved = credential() ?: return false
        if (presented?.length != 64) return false
        return MessageDigest.isEqual(saved.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8), presented.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8))
    }
    fun credential(): String? = preferences.getString(CREDENTIAL, null)
    fun rotate(): String {
        val bytes = ByteArray(32).also { SecureRandom().nextBytes(it) }
        val credential = bytes.joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it.toInt() and 255) }
        check(preferences.edit().putString(CREDENTIAL, credential).commit())
        return credential
    }
    fun setEnabled(enabled: Boolean) {
        require(!enabled || credential() != null) { "Create an automation credential before enabling" }
        check(preferences.edit().putBoolean(ENABLED, enabled).commit())
    }
    fun revoke() { check(preferences.edit().putBoolean(ENABLED, false).remove(CREDENTIAL).commit()) }
    companion object {
        private const val ENABLED = "notification_automation_enabled_v1"
        private const val CREDENTIAL = "notification_automation_credential_v1"
    }
}

/** Alarm/listener adapter. All policy and accounting belongs to the injected coordinator. */
@Singleton
class NotificationDeliveryEngine @Inject constructor(
    private val preferences: Preferences,
    private val coordinator: NotificationDeliveryCoordinator,
    private val deliveryScheduler: NotificationDeliveryScheduler,
) {
    suspend fun maintainDeliverySchedule(context: Context) {
        if (!preferences.isServiceEnabled()) return
        deliverPendingNotifications(context)
        deliveryScheduler.scheduleNextBoundaryDelivery(context)
    }
    suspend fun deliverPendingNotifications(context: Context) {
        if (preferences.isServiceEnabled()) coordinator.onBatchTick()
    }
}

Answers to your three questions (also going into the report), then I'll keep writing tests.

1. **Pointer loop.** Per gesture, not per frame: one `pointerInput` coroutine runs `editor.beginDrag(i, down.uptimeMillis)`. It then launches a single `editor.runDrag(channel, SystemClock::uptimeMillis)` against a `Channel.CONFLATED` channel, so it holds one latest position and never grows. Each move does `trySend`. Event time and `nowMillis` are the same uptime clock. Finger-up closes the channel, joins the loop, then calls `endDrag()`. Pointer-cancel or composition disposal runs `finally { channel.close(); abortDrag() }`. The tests drive `runDrag` with `runTest` virtual time and a real channel, not `holdTick` directly.
2. **Which schedule opens.** The editor opens on an explicit target. If today has a dated override, it opens on that one-date target. The header always names the target ("Every day" or "Only 2026-11-20"), and Apply writes exactly that target. Switching target is disabled while the draft is dirty. If storage changed since the editor loaded, Apply asks "Replace what is stored?" before writing. A repeating write says it also removes today's one-date schedule.

cd /home/mini/Documents/repos/Farhan/notification_filter && cat > AUTOMATION.md <<'EOF'
# Schedule automation

Change your notification schedule from Tasker, or from a shell with `adb`. The app receives one broadcast, checks it, and writes the schedule through the same path as the editor.

It is off until you turn it on in **Notification settings → Schedule automation**. Turning it on creates a credential (64 hex characters). Every request must carry it.

## Set up

1. Open **Notification settings → Schedule automation** and turn on **Allow automation**.
2. Tap **Copy** (or **Show**). Keep the credential private. **Rotate** replaces it; **Revoke** deletes it and turns automation off.
3. In Tasker, add a **Send Intent** action:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Action | `ly.com.tahaben.notification_filter.action.SET_SCHEDULE` |
| Extra | `credential:%FARHAN_CREDENTIAL` |
| Extra | `payload:%FARHAN_PAYLOAD` |
| Package | `ly.com.tahaben.farhan_alpha` |
| Class | `ly.com.tahaben.notification_filter_data.automation.ScheduleAutomationReceiver` |
| Target | Broadcast Receiver |

Store the credential in a Tasker variable that is not shared or logged, and build the JSON in `%FARHAN_PAYLOAD` before the action (Tasker splits an Extra at its first colon, so JSON in a variable is safest). The app only reads those two string extras. Android does not deliver implicit custom broadcasts to manifest receivers, so Package or Class is required.

Check the same request from a computer first (placeholders, not real values):

```sh
adb shell am broadcast \
  -n ly.com.tahaben.farhan_alpha/ly.com.tahaben.notification_filter_data.automation.ScheduleAutomationReceiver \
  -a ly.com.tahaben.notification_filter.action.SET_SCHEDULE \
  --es credential '<CREDENTIAL>' \
  --es payload '{"version":1,"windows":[{"start":0,"end":420,"budget":0},{"start":420,"end":1440,"budget":12}]}'
```

`am broadcast` prints `result=-1, data="accepted"` on success and `result=0, data="rejected:<ERROR>"` on failure.

## Payload

One JSON object, version 1.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `version` | integer | Must be `1`. |
| `mode` | string, optional | `"repeating"` (default) or `"dated"`. |
| `date` | string | Required for `"dated"`, forbidden for repeating. ISO local date, `YYYY-MM-DD`. |
| `windows` | array, 1 to 24 | The whole day, in order. |
| `windows[].start` | integer | Minute of the day the window starts, 0 to 1439. |
| `windows[].end` | integer | Minute it ends, 1 to 1440. 1440 is 24:00. |
| `windows[].budget` | integer | Points for the window, 0 or more. Any size is accepted. |

The windows must start at 0, end at 1440, touch with no gap or overlap, and each last at least 60 minutes. Numbers must be whole JSON integers: `5.0`, `"5"` and `true` are refused. Unknown fields are refused.

Examples:

```json
{"version":1,"windows":[{"start":0,"end":420,"budget":0},{"start":420,"end":1440,"budget":12}]}
```

```json
{"version":1,"mode":"dated","date":"2026-11-20","windows":[{"start":0,"end":600,"budget":0},{"start":600,"end":1440,"budget":10}]}
```

## What it changes

- **Repeating** replaces the every-day schedule. It also removes today's one-date schedule, so your change is not hidden. One-date schedules for future dates stay.
- **Dated** sets the schedule for that one date. Other dates use the every-day schedule. Dates before today are dropped whenever any schedule is saved.
- Points already spent in the current window are kept. Sending the same request again does not give them back.
- If you and automation both change a schedule, the last accepted change wins.
- A request that is refused changes nothing.

## Answers

- **Ordered broadcast** (`adb`, or Tasker when it waits for a result): result code `-1` and data `accepted`, or code `0` and data `rejected:<ERROR>`.
- **Settings screen**: the line under Schedule automation shows the last request, its time, and the error name. It never shows your credential or payload.

| Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `DISABLED` | Automation is off. Nothing is recorded. |
| `BAD_CREDENTIAL` | Wrong, missing or revoked credential. |
| `BUSY` | Two requests were already being handled. Nothing was read or changed. Wait a few seconds and send it again. |
| `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` | More than 4096 characters (at most 12 KiB as UTF-8), or more than 24 windows. |
| `MALFORMED_PAYLOAD` | Not the JSON above, or an unknown field. |
| `UNSUPPORTED_VERSION` | `version` is missing or not `1`. |
| `UNKNOWN_MODE` | `mode` is not `repeating` or `dated`. |
| `DATE_REQUIRED`, `MALFORMED_DATE`, `DATE_NOT_ALLOWED` | Date missing for dated, not a real date, or given for repeating. |
| `MALFORMED_WINDOW` | A window lacks a whole-number `start`, `end` or `budget`. |
| `INVALID_SCHEDULE` | Gap, overlap, a window under 60 minutes, or the day is not covered. |
| `STORAGE_FAILED` | Saving failed or the saved schedule needs repair. Nothing was changed. |

## Limits

- At most two requests are handled at once. Extra requests get `BUSY` straight away and are not queued, so retry them.
- The credential is a local key, not a login. Anyone who has it can change your schedule. It is not written to logs.
